subject: africanElephant
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: adult African bush elephant.
Style: low-poly.
reasoning:
I'm planning a low-poly adult African bush elephant model as a single TypeScript module using the SDK, aiming for 180-340 parts and 5-12 textures within a reasonable line budget, while making sure the code is complete and runs correctly.

I'm sketching the real-world proportions: shoulder height around 3 meters, body length about 6 meters, with a barrel-shaped torso, dipped back, columnar legs, large Africa-shaped ears, a long trunk, outward-curving tusks, and a thin tasseled tail, keeping the anatomy stylized but bold.

For the skin I'm planning grey-brown wrinkled texture with dusty ochre tones near the belly and head, using noise-based creases, small dark eyes, and ivory-colored tapered tusks swept along a curve. Now I'm working out the skeleton coordinates, placing the hip root joint and body center, then spacing the chest, rump, and head positions along the z-axis to match the elephant's overall length.

Next I'm plotting the full spine chain from rump through mid-back, shoulders, neck base, and into the head joint, then building a separate neck chain connecting the withers to the skull base. I'm sizing the head dome and setting ear placement on either side, with ears hanging from the upper head down past eye level, wider than tall, extending outward and downward from the skull.

Now I'm working out the trunk as a chain of tapering joints curving down from the face, narrowing from a wide base radius to a thin tip, with a slight upward curl near the ground. Then I move to the tusks, positioning them at the upper jaw sides and curving them outward, downward, then upward in the characteristic African elephant shape, roughly 1.4 meters long for an adult.

For the legs, I'm planning four pillar-like limbs positioned at the front and back of the body under the hip joints, with hidden knee bends to keep the stylized elephant silhouette sturdy and grounded.

I'm naming the chain joints shoulder, elbow, and ankle for each leg, setting the tip joint as the foot and marking the chain's role as "leg" so the limb system knows which end bears weight.

Now I'm thinking through the overall skeleton hierarchy: hips as the root joint with a spine role, then a spine chain running from the rump to the withers with three named spans, each leg chain parented appropriately off the hips or spine.

For the neck, I'm making a separate chain that starts where the spine chain ends, using the final spine joint as its parent rather than overlapping points. Then for the body itself, I'm planning a loft surface over the spine chain with stations at the rump, mid-body, shoulder, and chest, each defining a width and height so the mesh tapers correctly along the elephant's torso.

I'm working out the actual body dimensions now: rump around 1.5 wide by 2.2 tall, widening through the hips to roughly 2.1x2.5, then settling at the barrel where I'm reconsidering the center height and thickness so the belly sits near 1.2-1.3m off the ground while the back/withers reaches about 2.9-3.0m, giving a barrel height near 1.8m and a width around 1.7m so the legs at ±0.55-0.6 stay tucked inside the body silhouette.

I'm continuing through the remaining stations—rear, hips, barrel, and chest—adjusting each center height and width so the top profile smoothly slopes from the rump up through the shoulders and back down toward the chest, with the front chest station narrowing to about 1.2-1.6m wide where it'll transition into the neck and head.

Now I'm defining the spine chain as a catmull curve through these body centers, roughly level around y=2.1-2.3, that will drive the loft skinning and connect into a separate neck chain leading up to the head joint—keeping in mind the legs still need to attach properly along this same bone structure.

The legs will be separate chains with hip and shoulder joints positioned at (±0.55, 2.0, -1.0) and (±0.55, 2.0, 0.7), parented to the nearest spine joint so they move naturally with the body even though their absolute positions are set independently. Now I'm sketching out the overall plan: setting a scale constant for shoulder height, then building a skin color palette with dark/mid/dust tones plus pink accents for ears and trunk tip to capture that grey-brown dusty elephant look.

I'm defining additional palette colors for tusks (ivory with cream rings), toenails, dark eyes with iris highlights, tail tassel hairs, and pinkish mouth interior.

Writing the skin paint function...

Double-checking how the cells function returns distance values in grid units so the crack threshold scales correctly with cell size.

Thinking about performance: the paint function evaluates noise and cell patterns per texel across the atlas, with roughly 27 iterations for cell hashing plus several noise calls, applied over maybe a few hundred thousand texels at ~6.5mm resolution — should be acceptable given the elephant's surface area. I'm settling on cracked-plate skin texture since it matches elephant skin's natural look, then moving on to the body loft with spine bone chain.

For the loft stations I need an ordered array of position/width/height entries running rear to front along the bone chain. For the head, I'm weighing a sculpted sphere primitive (skull dome with scale) against a loft with stations positioned relative to the head joint, since the head needs distinct features like forehead bump and cheek bulges that a simple loft might not capture well.

I'm working out head loft station coordinates — back of skull, crown, forehead, and brow — adjusting their y/z positions and width/height so the crown tops out near 3.35, matching roughly how tall an elephant's head should sit above the shoulder line.

Now I'm figuring out how the neck connects the spine chain to the head, deciding whether to give the neck its own short chain or just merge it into a loft between the withers and the head base, and thinking about how a single-span neck chain would produce just one joint pointed at the head.

I'll have the body loft end around z 1.45 overlapping slightly with the head loft starting at z 1.35, which should hide any seam since the head mesh is wider anyway. Now I'm defining the skeleton itself, starting with the root hip joint and then the spine chain built from a sequence of catmull points running from the rear up toward the front.

I'm reconsidering whether the hips joint should sit mid-spine or actually be the first spine joint at the pelvis, since the SDK root must be the first parentless joint — maybe it's cleaner to place hips right at the rump point where the spine chain begins, so the chain is properly rooted there rather than floating as a separate parent.

Now I'm working out the leg placements: front legs run nearly straight from shoulder joints down to feet positioned slightly forward, with bone lengths just exceeding the root-to-target distance so they stay almost vertical with a small bend. Hind legs follow the same approach from hip joints, with feet placed a bit forward and bend directions set for the knee/hock to flex appropriately.

Working through foot geometry, I decide a tapered leg column ending in a rounded cap near y=0.25 gives a near-floor touch with negligible sink, which is acceptable within tolerance. So the leg shape itself can form the foot, avoiding needing a separate pad piece.

For toenails, I'm planning to use a ring arrangement of small cylinders placed around the foot's front axis, positioning them on the lower front face using angular range parameters to only cover the visible toe area rather than the whole circle.

Placing nail positions...

Positioning the foot cylinder so its tip aligns with the leg's end joint, then laying out nail positions in a row around the foot's front edge.

Still planning leg geometry...

To be safe, I'll just use `.at` to get the point, since that's the safer typed option even though I'm not fully certain how loft stations handle a ChainPoint directly.

Thinking about leg geometry more concretely, I'll go with a sweep approach instead of loft: using the leg chain as a path with a radius function tapering from a broad thigh (~0.42) down to a narrower ankle (~0.27-0.3), which gives smooth skin across the joints and matches elephant leg proportions.

I realize the leg top width at ±0.55 with radius 0.42 would poke slightly outside the body's barrel width (±0.92), so I'll tighten it to x=±0.5 with top radius 0.38 to keep legs tucked under the body. Checking the leg top's y-position confirms it sits inside the body silhouette correctly.

For the limb chain with a single knee joint, I need to pass bends as one direction — I'll use a nested list form `[[0, 0, -1]]` to match the expected type for a single inner joint.

The limb function returns three points (root, knee, foot) which I'll feed into a chain with three matching names, since a 3-name list correctly maps to two spans plus a tip. The sweep along this polyline will round the knee corner naturally as it builds the leg's skin.

Now I'm working out which spine segment should parent each leg chain, computing the z-coordinates along the spine path to find where the front legs should attach.

For the tail I'm laying out a thin chain curving down and back from the rump, with points dropping in height and shifting backward in z to roughly match an elephant tail reaching just past the hock.

Then I'm figuring out a tassel at the tip — a ring of dark hair-texture cards oriented along the tail's end frame to give it a tufted look.

I'll draw the tassel strands in greys so they pick up the tint from the color parameter, matching how cards get colored.

Now moving to the ears: big fan-shaped flaps sitting laterally at the sides of the head, extruded as flat sheets in the vertical-forward plane, hanging down and spreading outward in an Africa-shaped outline attached at the top to the head.

Still plotting ear outline points...

Checking proportions - the ear should span roughly 1.5m tall and 0.85-1.2m wide to match a real African elephant's big fan-shaped ear.

I'm plotting out the ear outline as a series of coordinate points forming the fan shape, with the top attached near the head and tapering to a point at the bottom.

Now I'm working out the ear's thickness, bevel, and placement relative to the head: positioning it at the sides, checking its range in z and y so it fits against the skull without colliding with the neck or shoulder.

I'm checking whether the hanging ear overlaps the shoulder region of the body, deciding that slight overlap looks natural since ears flap in front of shoulders anyway. Now I'm figuring out how to tilt the ear plane outward by adjusting its orientation vectors rather than using a separate rotation, working out the direction coefficients for each side.

I'm also settling the ear's attachment point on the head and thinking about how to color it—using a pinkish-grey base with a thin vein network generated through a cell-noise pattern for texture.

Skipping extra ear rim detailing to keep things simple, and moving on to placing the eyes: small, positioned near the sides of the head under the brow, roughly where the front-top of the head meets the face.

I'm thinking through how to render each eye as a decal on the curved head surface — a dark iris with a lid line and a small highlight, drawn via SVG and projected outward on the +X/-X side facing direction, applied onto the head loft mesh.

I'm now working out the orientation logic: the decal's "dir" sets which way it faces outward from the surface, and since the model faces +Z, I need to figure out which way is the viewer's "right" and "up" when looking at the left flank from the +X side so the eye drawing mirrors correctly on each side.

For positioning the eyes, I'm placing the decal point just inside the skull's surface along the dir axis so the projection lands correctly on the head at the right station.

I'll keep elephant eyes small, around 0.1x0.075, using the decal alone without a separate sphere.

Now I'm working out the trunk's attachment: the head joint sits near the neck top aimed forward-down, and the trunk chain starts from a separate point on the face as a child of that head joint rather than at the joint's own position.

For the trunk path, I'm sketching a curve from the base under the face down toward the ground, tapering and curling slightly back near the tip rather than looping fully, with radius shrinking from about 0.24 at the base to roughly 0.07 near the end.

I'm also thinking about tiny finger-like lobes at the trunk's very tip, deciding whether to add wrinkle rings along the sweep, and planning to make the trunk a bendable chain of joints parented to the head rather than a rigid shape.

I'll tag the trunk's role as "tentacle" since it's a boneless, bendable appendage, and lay out six points across five spans for the chain. Then I'm sweeping the trunk with a tapering radius from base to tip, and checking that the trunk's base position actually sits correctly embedded within the head's facial geometry rather than floating outside it, comparing the brow and forehead loft heights at that z-position to make sure they overlap properly.

Now I'm designing the tusks: curving bezier paths emerging from the upper jaw, bending outward and forward then sweeping up at the tip like an African elephant's, with tapering radius from a thick buried base to a narrow tip, and checking spacing so tusks don't collide with the trunk.

For material, I'm painting ivory tones with subtle growth-ring striations along the tusk length, possibly darkening slightly near the tip for realism.

Next I'm moving to the lower jaw, planning a small loft shape beneath the trunk to form the chin area of the mouth.

I'll keep the jaw simple since it's mostly hidden under the trunk anyway—just a small chin loft in skin color with a jaw joint role, not worrying much about mouth interior detail. Moving on to head decorations like the forehead wrinkles.

I'm adding dust and mud paint effects on the legs blended toward a mud color near the ground, plus toenails on the hind feet. For sparse body hair, I'll scatter a modest number of bristle cards on the crown of the head to mimic the sparse hair African elephants actually have, keeping the count low for realism.

I'm skipping ground elements and extra skin-fold details like armpit folds or toe pads, focusing instead on palette choices—grey body with warm dust tones, pinkish-grey veined ears, ivory tusks with warm banding, ivory nails, and dark brown eyes with a white highlight. I'm also tallying the texture budget: eye SVG, painted ear veins, tassel and bristle textures, and nail material.

Now I'm reviewing the builder API signatures I'll need—joint, chain, sweep, loft, part, stick, cards, decal, surface, ring, along, sprout, limb, region, pose, extrude, lathe, membrane, slab, rod/capsule/spike, frustumBox, segments—to make sure I use them correctly before writing the actual construction code.

Still cataloging builder API signatures...

Now I'm checking outline point typing for the extrude function, confirming frame/line/rng/noise/cells/mix/smoothstep/paint/svg imports from the math module, and verifying that paint callbacks returning Rgb satisfy ColorInput. I'm starting to define hide/skin color constants for the paint function.

Still writing skin paint...

I'm also estimating performance cost: with noise and cell evaluations running per texel across up to a million pixels, the baked texture generation should take a few seconds but stay within acceptable limits.

For the ear paint, I'm mixing a base ear color with a pink tone using noise, then adding subtle vein patterns via cell distance functions in surface coordinates, keeping in mind ears are lit from behind in real elephants. Now I'm moving on to sketching the eye texture as an SVG.

I'm drawing concentric ellipses for the eye: a dark rim, a brown iris, a black pupil, and a small white highlight for specularity. I'm reconsidering whether the transparent areas outside the ellipse should reveal skin underneath or if I need an opaque eyelid ring instead, so I'm adding an outer eyelid-crease colored ellipse before the iris to avoid awkward cutouts.

Actually, since the decal sits directly on the surface itself, cutting away transparent corners just reveals the head's own skin underneath rather than creating a hole—so the eye decal's transparent corners are safe to use.

For the eye, I'll draw an ellipse with eyelid ring, brown iris, pupil, and a small highlight. For bristle texture I'm sketching a small SVG with a few curved dark strand paths in grays for tinting, and similarly for the tassel texture I'm drawing several curved strands across a taller viewBox to simulate hanging fibers.

For toenails, I'm making flattened ivory spheres scaled thinner in one axis and attaching them to the foot bone. Now I'm working out the crown bristles -- scattering hits across the skull surface filtered to the top region, then generating cards with a lean angle and an upward-backward flow direction so they tilt correctly, using a seeded RNG and minimum distance for even spacing.

For the tail, I'm laying out a catmull-rom spline from the rump down to around hock height, checking that the root sits inside the rump loft and the tip length matches a realistic elephant tail. Now I'm checking the hind leg joint placement, measuring the vertical span from hip to ankle to make sure the leg length is proportional.

Now checking the front leg similarly, then verifying foot cylinder proportions against the leg's tapering radius, and finally comparing leg attachment width against the barrel's half-width at that height to make sure the legs don't clip outside the body silhouette.

I'm also running through the body loft stations - tail base, hips, barrel, chest, and shoulder/neck - adjusting their widths and heights so the top and bottom profile heights line up with elephant proportions, tweaking a few centers where values came out too tall.

Now I'm defining the spine joint chain from tail to shoulders, then continuing into a separate neck chain of two joints leading up to the head joint, making sure the head's bone pose and aim direction are set for forward-slightly-down posture.

For the body loft itself, I'm matching the catmull sweep path through six stations approximately to the spine chain's joint positions, accepting a slight mismatch since the spine chain only passes through five points while the loft uses six stations.

For the head, I'm placing loft stations down the length—from the base at z=1.55 to the rounded front tip at z=2.8—with widths tapering from about 1.0 down to 0.66 near the nose, giving it a rounded cap. Checking the eye placement at (0.56, 2.8, 2.2) via decal projection, I realize the ear geometry (spanning z 1.23–2.47) actually overlaps that region and would cover the eye, which is a problem I need to fix.

I'm repositioning the ear origin further back to z≈1.5–1.55 so its front edge sits around z=2.12–2.15, clearing space for the eye at z=2.3. I'm also checking that the ear's inner attachment aligns with the head's width at that height (~0.5 half-width) and that the tilt keeps the ear's base properly flush against the head without the ear ballooning wider than the head or body near the shoulder.

There's some minor overlap between the ear's lower-back region and the front leg's shoulder area, but since ears naturally drape over the shoulder, I'll accept this intersection as visually fine. The ear's plane sits laterally at the head's side (x≈0.5) and extends back over the neck in the z-direction, which matches how real ears are positioned.

Checking the tusk roots near the brow and face region, I confirm they sit inside the head volume and project forward past the face, which is correct. But the tusk base at x≈0.22 with its radius overlaps the trunk base radius at z≈2.7, so I need to check how far that intersection extends along the trunk's path.

The trunk tapers from radius 0.24 down by 0.17 per unit of its path parameter, and comparing cross-sections shows the tusks clear the trunk at z≈3.0+ since the trunk narrows faster than the tusks spread outward — only minor overlap near the base, which reads naturally as tusks emerging around the trunk.

Now I'm laying out the trunk's catmull-rom control points, curving it down and forward from the head, forward to a peak extension around z=3.25, then curling back down toward a tip near the ground, checking that it clears the head's front profile as it exits.

I'm naming the trunk's six path points into five bone segments, then designing the tusk as a bezier curve with four control points that sweep outward, downward, and finally curl up and inward at the tip to mimic a natural tusk shape, verifying it stays clear of the trunk's radius at every z-level.

Defining tusk radius function...

Then I'm working on the jaw: placing a small chin joint under the trunk root, lofting three stations to form the lower jaw mass, and rigging it to the jaw bone with an aim toward the trunk tip.

Now I'm setting up the hip root joint and spine chain, then figuring out which spine joint should parent the front and hind leg chains — using spine.joints[3] for the shoulders and spine.joints[1] for the hips. I'm also naming the leg joints with an "L"/"R" suffix based on side, and making sure all joint names across trunk, neck, tail, and ear chains stay unique and valid.

I'm then checking name clashes across the full skeleton, building sweeps for the legs and tail using the chain's parametric points, and working out how to create a tail-tip tassel ring by sampling a point near the end of the tail chain and feeding it into a line/ring construct.

Figuring out the ring's tilt so the tassel items flare downward along the tail's tangent direction rather than sticking out oddly.

Then building cards from those ring items with a downward lean and flow, sized to about 0.3m to match a realistic elephant tail tassel, rooted at the correct radius on the tapered tail tip.

Now I'm working out foot placement—cylindrical foot shapes attached to each leg's tip joint with an appropriate vertical offset.

For toenails, I'm computing positions around the front arc of each foot using an angular spread, placing small flattened spheres near the base of each foot to mimic toenails, scaled down vertically for a nail-like shape.

I decide to use geometry.scale() directly on the sphere geometry rather than risk unsupported scale options in b.part, then colored them ivory. Front feet get four nails spread across a wider arc, hind feet get four across a tighter arc.

Moving on to other body details I might add—skin folds, trunk wrinkles, and the dark temporal gland patch near the head—to push the realism further.

I decide to skip the temporal gland since positioning it cleanly is too fiddly, and skip eyelashes too. For the head, the dome shape already comes from the loft, so that's covered. I'll focus remaining effort on trunk tip detail, adding two small finger-like lobes at the very end of the trunk since that's a key elephant identity cue alongside the big ears, tusks, and wrinkled skin.

I'm extending the trunk chain to six joints so there's a proper tip joint, then attaching two tiny sphere lobes near the tip to suggest the finger-like grasping tip. I'll also include tail bristles, and tally up the part count across body, head, jaw, legs, feet, and nails to make sure the total stays reasonable.

For textures, I'm settling on just a few key ones—eye, bristle, tassel—and considering whether to add an ear detail or a subtle pink mouth line for extra richness, though I may skip these as unnecessary. I'm also thinking through how to shade the inner ear surface differently from the outer, using the face normal direction to decide which side gets the lighter tone.

For the ear's physical shape, I'm deciding on extrude depth and bevel size, and weighing whether to apply corner-smoothing on the outline—worried that smoothing could cause edge-crossing errors on a non-convex shape, so I'm leaning toward adding more outline points instead and keeping smoothing off for safety.

Writing ear outline coordinates...

I'll set ear thickness with a taper from thin at the bottom (0.03) to thicker at the attachment point (0.08), plus a small bevel, and bind the ears explicitly to the head bone rather than relying on the nearest joint. For the body, I'm thinking of adding a wow factor with ochre dust-patch blotches on the head and back using noise, mimicking how African elephants dust themselves reddish-brown.

Writing SKIN paint function...

I'm checking that the cell-based seam pattern for skin plates and the ochre/belly/mud color blending all use properly typed smoothstep and mix calls returning valid color types.

Now I'm picking colors for the hide, seam, ochre, belly, and mud tones, then setting up the ear's paint function with an inner pink gradient and a vein network derived from cell borders, before moving on to the tusk's ivory material.

Adding ring bands to ivory tusk shading, then starting an SVG definition for the eye shape with an ellipse outline.

Still writing bristle SVG...

Scattering bristles across the skull surface, filtering hits by normal and height to target the crown area, then placing bristle cards with lean and flow parameters for a tufted look.

I'm checking the tail tassel ring placement at the tip, verifying tilt and count work with the frame orientation, then double-checking that all ground contact points—feet, trunk tip, tail tassel—sit correctly at or above y=0 so nothing clips through the ground.

Now I'm comparing the overall height against real elephant proportions, confirming the shoulder and crown heights match an adult African bush elephant's ~3-3.2m scale. I'm defining the body loft stations from rump through hips, barrel, chest, shoulder, and neck top, assigning widths and heights at each station and binding the loft to the spine and neck bones for deformation.

I realize the loft's default rounded end caps will extend the body beyond the path endpoints by roughly the end radius, which could push the rump too far back near the tail and the neck too far forward — so I need to either shift the stations or specify flat caps at the rear to keep proportions correct, while letting the rounded front cap stay hidden inside the head geometry.

I'll go with a flat start cap and round end cap for the rear rounding, trusting it'll mostly stay hidden near the tail root. For the front and head junctions, I'm checking that the neck's rounded cap tucks inside the head geometry so it stays concealed, and similarly verifying the head's back station cap nests inside the neck region without poking through.

I'm reworking the face stations so the front cap doesn't overshoot past the trunk — pulling the final station back to around z 2.62 with a smaller radius so the bulge lands near the tusk root zone instead of sticking out too far. I'm adjusting the full set of head stations (positions, widths, heights) to get a smoother taper down to where the trunk emerges, then setting the back cap to rounded.

Checking whether the head's back dome at z 1.5 overlaps the neck loft cross-section — the cross-sections are close enough in size that I'd risk z-fighting if I use a flat cap there, so I'll just use the default rounded cap to let it sink into the neck seamlessly.

Now I'm laying out the jaw loft stations with their own widths/heights and round caps, picking a muted skin tone for the lower jaw, and noticing the jaw tip and head front cap positions are close enough that they'll overlap slightly — which should be fine for blending the two shapes together.

Next I'm checking the trunk root placement against the chin and jaw geometry — it overlaps the jaw's top region, which is fine since the jaw sits inside the trunk base. Then I work out where the tusk should emerge from the face by comparing its root coordinates to the head's loft cross-section at that z-depth, adjusting the root position slightly so it falls safely inside the head surface, and sketching out a curved tusk path from root through two control points to a tip, with a base radius wide enough to bury the cap into the head. I also double check the eye position against the head surface at that z-depth to confirm it sits right on the face, then move on to the mouth, leg stance positions, and start writing the leg code.

Writing leg-building helper...

Placing the nail positions on the foot cylinder's surface, then flattening sphere geometry along z so each nail just protrudes slightly from the toe surface.

I'm defining the six trunk segment names mapping to control points P0 through P5, checking that the tip's tangent curls down and back plausibly like a real trunk curl. Then I'm placing small sphere "finger" details near the tip in local model coordinates, and double-checking the trunk sweep cap radii and wrinkle painting before moving on to tusks, ears, and leg parenting.

Now I'm verifying the spine/neck/head joint chain: front and hind legs parent to specific spine joints, the neck is built from a catmull curve through three points giving two named segments, and the head joint aims forward from the neck's end toward a point near the face. I'm also checking the jaw joint's aim direction, confirming tusks and the trunk chain parent correctly to the head joint, and setting up the root hips joint at the base of the spine.

I'm working through the body loft stations defining the rump's cross-sectional width, height, and placement to shape the back end of the creature's torso.

Then I lay out the spine path points and confirm the hips root position, before checking that the front legs line up under the chest station and that the tail root sits inside the rump's radius.

Working through the hind leg geometry, I set the root and target positions and verify the segment lengths cover the needed distance with a slight forward bend for the knee. I do the same for the front legs, placing the elbow bend backward, and check the foot cylinder placement and nail orientation for both front and hind feet.

For the leg sweep caps, I'm checking if the rounded cap at the foot tip sinks below ground level — it's about 6cm, right at the edge of the allowed 2% tolerance — so I consider switching the sweep's end cap to flat instead of round to keep it hidden inside the foot cylinder.

With trunk, ears, tusks, and tail capped off, I'm positioning the ears relative to the head bone, checking the attachment point and outline extend outward over the shoulder area without clipping issues, then placing the eye decals symmetrically on the skull with outward-facing directions mirrored for left and right sides.

I'm scattering bristles across the top of the skull, filtering so they only land on the upper surface, then moving on to define the color palette — hide tones, seams, ochre shading, belly and nail colors, and the ivory tusk shades with their highlight variants.

Now I'm writing the ear paint function, blending a base and inner tone based on how much the surface faces inward, then layering a cellular vein pattern tinted with the vein color to mimic ear vasculature.

I'm moving on to the tusk ivory paint, adding faint growth-ring striping using a sine pattern along the tusk length and darkening the tip slightly, then setting up the body skin paint to eventually layer in mud staining based on height.

Now I'm weighing whether the module is long enough relative to the suggested 700-1100 line target — since the elephant is fairly complex, I'm planning to add extra surface detail like trunk wrinkle rings, ear folds, toenails, tail hair, belly folds, a dorsal fold line, eyelashes, mouth line, and a temporal dark patch to push toward a richer "wow" result rather than stopping at a bare-bones mesh.

I'm going through several candidate details — lash spikes, ear fold sweeps, brow ridge creases, knee/elbow wrinkle bands, a dark mouth line under the trunk, temporal gland spots — and deciding most aren't worth the complexity, settling on a moderately sized module around 400 lines while prioritizing code correctness. I'm setting up the meta export with the elephant's name and description, then starting the default build function and initializing the builder.

I'm verifying structural details: loft stations stay monotone in z across the body, head, and jaw sections, the loft bone option correctly chains to the spine/neck and head joint, and the head joint's parent correctly references the neck chain's joint. Now I'm defining the nail geometry using scaled, rotated sphere shapes for each toe.

I'm also working through the limb function's parameters—passing root and target as point arrays, lengths as a tuple, and bends as a direction list—checking that the type system accepts these literal array forms as valid Point and Direction inputs, and considering whether to explicitly type my vectors using the SDK's exported V3 type.

I'm also checking that Joint imports from the SDK correctly, then thinking through how to position a ring geometry along the tail—weighing whether using raw Vector3 points (which lack bone association) versus using chain-derived points would correctly attach the geometry to the nearest joint rather than defaulting unpredictably.

I'm confirming the cards and bristles options are using valid SDK parameters like vary, rng, color, lean, and flow, then sketching out similar card settings for the tassel geometry with a downward flow direction.

Checking the sweep and bezier calls for tusks look right with four control points and a tapering radius function, then I'm mapping out the remaining body parts—tusks, ears, eyes, and legs—as mirrored loops over symmetric positions.

Now I'm starting the actual module, confirming the right imports (bezier, catmull, cells, paint, rng, svg, and the Rgb/Joint types) are pulled from the builder package, then setting up the metadata description for the elephant and defining the color palette for hide, seams, ivory, and mud tones.

Writing color palette constants...

Now I'm writing the paint function for the skin, layering procedural noise for grain texture, cell patterns to carve wrinkle-like seams between hide plates, ochre dust highlights on the upper body, a lighter belly tone, and muddy coloring on the lower legs, double-checking that each smoothstep blend only applies where intended.

Then I move on to defining flat colors for feet, nails, jaw, and other parts, confirming I'm staying within the color budget, before starting the skeleton build—setting up the hip joint, a spine chain following a catmull-rom curve through several control points, and beginning a neck chain extending upward from the spine's end.
